<reason>A built a tight case anchored directly in the resolution's key phrase "solely because": vouchers are a proxy for a protected/disadvantaged class, and the harm-cost asymmetry justifies a bright line. B's best material was the genuinely distinct claim that accepting a voucher means entering a separate contractual relationship with a third-party agency (inspections, HAP contracts, approval delays), which is grounded in real program mechanics and forced A to sharpen the "otherwise qualified" boundary. But this distinction never escaped the core problem A exploited: if the "contractual objection" applies uniformly to every voucher holder regardless of individual merit, it is functionally indistinguishable from rejecting "solely because" of the voucher, which is exactly what the resolution targets. A's closing turned B's own words in B4.6 into an explicit confession of this uniform, class-wide effect, and B's closing reply (the objection "follows the contract, not the tenant") restated the distinction without resolving why that isn't just relabeled proxy exclusion. B did expose a real tension in A's position (timing-based exclusion is permitted, contract-based is not) that A's closing didn't fully address, keeping the debate competitive, but overall A's route more directly answered the resolution as written and landed the more damaging late rebuttal.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing move recasting B's B4.6 admission ("uniform effect... without resting on judgment about voucher holders' character") as itself the definition of proxy discrimination the resolution is meant to stop, which B's final reply did not neutralize.</best_rebuttal>
